title: When the Weather Falls
premise: Wren Brightwater, a piano tuner who inherited their grandmother Odile's crumbling house, has always treated the place like a rental they can't quite leave. When a late-night radio broadcast plays a song Odile wrote and never recorded — performed by a stranger claiming authorship — Wren begins tuning the house itself, coaxing its radiators, floorboards, and forgotten piano to yield the truth of who Odile loved and what she surrendered. The trail leads to Elias Vann, the man in the old photographs whom family legend cast as a villain, now dying in a coastal town two hundred miles away. As Wren uncovers that Odile gave away both the song and her heart to protect her sister's marriage, they must choose between preserving the family's loyal fiction and telling the truth that could free everyone, including themselves. In the end, Wren records the song at last in the house where it was written, forgives the stranger in the photographs, and finally signs their name to the deed — as an owner, not a tenant.
about_author: Juniper Dravenmoor is a former piano restorer who spent a decade tuning instruments in houses older than their owners, collecting the stories walls keep. 'When the Weather Falls' is their second novel, written mostly in winter, in a house that hums.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Key
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Establishes Wren's itinerant life tuning pianos across the city while technically owning Odile's house, which they visit monthly but never sleep in overnight. The radiators knock out rhythms Wren half-recognizes. Emotional beat: quiet displacement, the ache of inheriting something you refuse to inhabit.

chapters.title: A Song Out of Season
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Driving home from a job, Wren hears a radio performance of 'Weatherfall' — a melody only ever heard once, played by Odile on the parlor piano when Wren was nine. The announcer credits composer Elias Vann. Wren pulls over, shaking. Beat: the past puncturing the present without warning.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, first night actually spent in the house. Wren tunes Odile's neglected upright and notices the radiator's knocking matches the song's opening phrase. Searching the attic yields a locked writing desk and a photograph of Odile laughing beside a stranger — Elias. Beat: curiosity overtaking grief.

chapters.title: The Sister Who Stayed Silent
chapters.summary: Wren visits Great-Aunt Marguerite, Odile's younger sister, sharp-tongued in a care facility. Marguerite insists Elias was 'a thief of small things' and warns Wren off digging. She slips, though: mentions a summer at Graywater Cove. Beat: loyalty deployed as a wall; first hint of a cover story.

chapters.title: Letters Under the Damper
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Following the radiator's rhythm, Wren finds letters hidden inside the boiler room wall — unsigned, passionate, dated 1962, addressed only to 'O.' They stop abruptly after one final letter that reads like a goodbye. Beat: intimacy with the dead; the love affair becomes undeniable.

chapters.title: Graywater Cove
chapters.summary: Wren travels to the coastal town, following a return address on the last letter. The boarding house where Elias lived is now a shuttered inn run by his niece, Sable Vann, who recognizes the handwriting instantly. Beat: entering enemy territory and finding unexpected warmth.

chapters.title: The Man in the Photograph
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. She describes her uncle Elias: a composer who never wrote again after one summer, who kept a woman's glove in a drawer for sixty years. He is alive but fading in a nursing home, losing words daily. Beat: the villain dissolving into a grieving man; Wren's certainty cracks.

chapters.title: Words Like Weather
chapters.summary: Wren meets Elias, who mistakes them for Odile for one devastating moment before surfacing. He can no longer finish sentences but plays fragments flawlessly. When Wren hums 'Weatherfall,' he weeps and says, 'She gave it away. Ask her why.' Beat: tenderness across time; the mystery deepens rather than resolves.

chapters.title: The Radio Man's Regret
chapters.summary: Wren tracks down the radio producer who aired the song. It came from a donated reel-to-reel tape labeled in Elias's hand — meaning Elias recorded it decades ago and released it only now, near death, as a claim or a confession. Beat: the stakes sharpen; someone wanted this heard before it was too late.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Version
chapters.summary: Alternating POV, Marguerite in 1962 (rendered as her fractured telling). A young Marguerite, pregnant and unmarried, faced ruin; Odile ended things with Elias and let him take the blame publicly to shield the family name. Beat: sympathy for the liar; loyalty revealed as sacrifice, not just betrayal.

chapters.title: Odile's Desk Opens
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Back home, the writing desk's lock finally gives — inside, Odile's unfinished memoir and the original manuscript of 'Weatherfall,' annotated in two hands, hers and Elias's. They wrote it together. Beat: the song was shared property; the theft narrative collapses entirely.

chapters.title: What Duty Costs
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confronts Marguerite with the memoir. Marguerite breaks down: Odile chose her sister over her love and never regretted it aloud, though the house's every pipe grieved. Marguerite begs Wren not to tell Elias the truth before he dies. Beat: the central conflict crystallizes — protection versus honesty.

chapters.title: Sable's Claim
chapters.summary: Sable's POV. Sable reveals the family wants credit for Elias's legacy and plans to publish 'his' song with a fabricated history. She asks Wren to stay silent about Odile for the sake of a clean story. Beat: Wren sees their own temptation mirrored — the comfortable lie offered twice.

chapters.title: The Tuner's Dilemma
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, alone in the house through a storm. The radiators fall silent for the first time, as if the house is holding its breath. Wren realizes they've been a tenant of their own grief, avoiding Odile's choices by avoiding the house. Beat: dark night of the soul; the personal stakes surface.

chapters.title: A Truth Half-Sung
chapters.summary: Wren returns to Graywater Cove intending to tell Elias everything, but he's had a stroke; music is now his only fluent language. Wren plays the manuscript's harmony line while Elias sings the melody, and in the collaboration Wren understands: the truth can be given as music, not just testimony. Beat: reframing forgiveness as transmission.

chapters.title: The Deed and the Debt
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Legal complication: Sable's family contests nothing yet, but a journalist sniffing around threatens to expose the story as scandal. Wren must decide whether to go public with the co-authorship or let the lie calcify into history. Beat: rising external pressure converging with internal choice.

chapters.title: Marguerite at the Piano
chapters.summary: Wren brings Marguerite to the house — her first visit in forty years. Marguerite touches the keys and confesses fully, on a voice memo she asks Wren to keep 'for whoever needs it after.' Beat: the loyalist choosing truth at last; generational guilt handed down and transformed.

chapters.title: Recording the House
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren sets up microphones through the rooms and records 'Weatherfall' as the house performs it — radiators, wind in the chimney, the tuned upright — layering Odile's and Elias's voices back into the song. Beat: climax of craft; the house becomes the duet it always was.

chapters.title: Last Broadcast
chapters.summary: Elias's deathbed scene, partly Sable's POV. Wren plays the recording for him; hearing Odile's harmonies, he speaks her name clearly for the first time in months and dies that night, at peace. Beat: emotional climax; forgiveness delivered in sound rather than argument.

chapters.title: The Story Goes Out
chapters.summary: Wren releases the recording and the true history — co-authorship, sacrifice, and all — refusing both families' tidy fictions. Some praise it, some rage. Marguerite, listening, says only, 'She would have hated it and needed it equally.' Beat: consequences accepted; truth chosen over comfort.

chapters.title: Signing the House
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren repairs the house properly — boiler, roof, the piano restrung — and moves in, unpacking boxes left sealed for years. On the deed copy pinned above the desk, Wren writes their own name beneath Odile's. Beat: inheritance reclaimed; tenant becomes owner of house and history alike.

chapters.title: When the Weather Falls
chapters.summary: Epilogue, Wren's POV, one year later. First autumn rain; the radio plays 'Weatherfall' again, now credited to O. Brightwater and E. Vann. A young musician arrives for lessons, having heard the house's version. Wren opens the door. Beat: resolution and continuation — the song, like the house, passed on intact and true.
